1.title: every tradition starts here
1.hook: every tradition starts here; before the words, before the books
1.carry: someone is in there — say hi
1.howItsDone: Many paths begin with the breath: Buddhist and Hindu teachers teach watching the breath, yoga has breathing practices called pranayama, and many people of every faith take one slow breath before they pray or sit.

segments.voice: Before anything else, notice something. You're breathing. You were breathing before you opened this, you'll be breathing after you close it, and you almost never think about it. Every tradition on earth starts here. Before the books, before the words, before anyone argued about anything, there was a person sitting still, feeling the air go in and out. Monks do it. Grandmothers do it at the kitchen table. Basketball players do it before a free throw. This path is for people who don't belong to one religion, or who belong to a few, or who aren't sure yet. So we start with the one thing every single one of us already does. Today's word is breathe.
screen: `YOU'RE BREATHING.` → `BEFORE THE WORDS, BEFORE THE BOOKS.` → `EVERY TRADITION STARTS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise hiding inside it. In language after language, the word for breath and the word for spirit started out as the same word. In Latin, spiritus means breath. It comes from spirare, to breathe. That's where English gets spirit, and also inspire, which once meant to breathe into, and expire, to breathe out for the last time. In Greek, pneuma means wind, breath and spirit. In Hebrew, ruach does the same. In Sanskrit, the old language of India, prana is breath and the life that rides on it. In Chinese thought there's qi, a word that began with vapor and breath. Each of these words grew up in its own language, and each tradition tells its own story about it. But they all looked at the same thing, a body that breathes and a body that doesn't, and named the difference with the word for air. The Bible tells it in its second chapter. In the King James words: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." That's one tradition's picture, and it deserves to be heard as its own. There's a plainer side too. Breath is the one part of your body that runs by itself and also takes orders. You can't slow your heart just by deciding to. You can slow your breath, and a long, easy breath out tends to settle the body. That's well studied, and it needs no belief to work. So the oldest spiritual word is also the most practical one.

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Sit however you're sitting. Breathe in slowly, all the way, and feel where the air goes: nose, chest, belly. Then let it out, a little longer than it came in. That's all. Nothing to believe, nothing to say. One breath, the oldest practice there is, and you just did it on purpose.
Breathe. The word underneath spirit, in Latin and Greek, in Hebrew and Sanskrit. The thing you've done since before you had a name. First word on your strand.

2.title: pascal: the quiet room
2.hook: Pascal: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber (Pensées 139, Trotter's 1910 translation)
2.tomorrow: attention is the only thing you actually own
2.howItsDone: Many traditions have a practice of simply sitting still: Zen Buddhists sit zazen, often facing a wall; Quakers gather in silent worship; and many people keep a few quiet minutes alone at the start or end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was breathe. Your line: someone is in there, say hi. Did you catch yourself breathing, even once? That counts. Day two.

Try this, just in your head. You're in a plain room. No phone. No book. Nobody else. Nothing to do for fifteen minutes. How long before you reach for something? Researchers at the University of Virginia tried a version of this in 2014. They left people alone with nothing but their thoughts and a button that gave a mild electric shock. People who had already tried the shock, and said they'd pay to avoid it, still pushed the button: most of the men, and about a quarter of the women. Anything, rather than just sitting. More than three hundred and fifty years earlier, a French mathematician saw this coming. Today's word is sit.
screen: `A PLAIN ROOM. NOTHING TO DO.` → `A BUTTON.` → `ANYTHING BUT SITTING.`

segments.voice: His name was Blaise Pascal. As a young man he built one of the first mechanical calculators and did serious work on probability. Then, after an intense religious experience, he spent his last years writing notes toward a defense of Christian faith. He died at thirty-nine, before he finished, and his friends published the notes. We call them the Pensées, the thoughts. You've probably seen one of them on a poster: all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone. That's a modern paraphrase. It's close, but it isn't what the old translation says. In W. F. Trotter's 1910 English, Pascal writes: "I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." Not problems. Unhappiness. And listen to his reason. The same note walks through gambling, war, the royal court, hunting. A man will chase a hare all day, Pascal says, that he wouldn't take if you handed it to him. He doesn't want the hare. He wants the chase, because it keeps him from thinking about himself. Pascal's own answer to what waits in that quiet room was a Christian one, and it deserves to be read on its own terms someday. But his observation stands by itself: the restlessness isn't a sign something is wrong with you. He saw it in everyone. Zen Buddhism, in Japan, has a whole practice built around sitting, called zazen, seated meditation. The teacher Dogen taught a form called shikantaza, just sitting: no goal, nothing to win. You sit, and the restlessness comes and goes like anything else. Pascal and Dogen had very different reasons, and neither needs the other. But both noticed the chair.
screen: `PASCAL AND HIS PENSÉES.` · `THE POSTER LINE IS A PARAPHRASE.` · `THE HARE HE WOULDN'T TAKE.` · `ZEN: JUST SITTING.` · then, large: `THEY CANNOT STAY QUIETLY IN THEIR OWN CHAMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. One breath, with the bell, and one small experiment. Put the phone face down if you can, or just let your hands rest. Sit. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out. And notice the tiny pull to do something else. You don't have to fight it, and you don't have to obey it. Just notice it's there. That pull is exactly what Pascal was writing about. You just sat with it for one whole breath.
Sit. The simplest instruction there is, and somehow one of the hardest. Not to do anything. Just to stay. Second word.
Your line: sit anyway. Once today, when you're waiting, in a line, at a red light, for a kettle, don't reach for anything. Sit anyway, for the length of one breath. Day two.

3.title: attention is the only thing you actually own
3.hook: attention is the only thing you actually own
3.tomorrow: the rule that keeps turning up
3.howItsDone: Buddhist mindfulness practice trains attention by resting it on something simple, often the breath, and gently bringing it back each time it wanders; many other traditions use a word, a sound or a candle flame the same way.

segments.voice: Two words in. Breathe, and sit. Your line was sit anyway. Did you manage one breath of waiting without reaching for anything? Or did the pull win? Both tell you something. Day three.

Think about what's asking for your attention right now. The screen in your hand. A notification you haven't opened. Something someone said this morning that you're still turning over. Whole companies are built to win a few more seconds of it, and they're very good at their jobs. You can lose money and earn it back. You can lose a day, and there's another one tomorrow. But the thing you're spending, all day long, is attention. Today starts with a bold claim: attention is the only thing you actually own. Let's see if it holds up. Today's word is notice.
screen: `WHAT'S ASKING FOR YOU RIGHT NOW?` → `EVERYONE WANTS A FEW SECONDS.` → `THE THING YOU'RE SPENDING.`

segments.voice: In 1890 the American psychologist William James published a huge book, The Principles of Psychology. In the chapter on attention he wrote a line that sounds simple and isn't: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Not what happens to you. What you attend to. Two people can sit through the same dinner and go home with two different evenings, because they noticed different things. James also saw that attention wanders, all the time, and that bringing it back is the real skill. He wrote that "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." Over and over again. Not once. That matters, because most people who try to pay attention think the wandering means they failed. For James, the coming back was the whole thing. Buddhism has a word for this, from Pali, the language of its early texts: sati. It's usually translated mindfulness, but it comes from a root that means to remember. Remembering to come back to what's here. Buddhist teachers build a whole path of practice around it. And the Greek teacher Epictetus, who was born enslaved, taught his students to sort everything into two piles: what's up to us, and what isn't. Your body, your reputation, what other people do: not up to you, he said. Your own judgments and choices: up to you. Three voices, three different reasons, and none of them needs the others. So, is attention really the only thing you own? Maybe not the only thing. But it may be the one you can take back fastest. You just did, by listening.
screen: `WHAT I AGREE TO ATTEND TO.` · `BRINGING IT BACK, OVER AND OVER.` · `SATI: REMEMBERING TO COME BACK.` · `WHAT'S UP TO US, AND WHAT ISN'T.` · then, large: `THE ONE YOU CAN TAKE BACK FASTEST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first breath, notice one thing you can hear. Just one. On the second breath, notice one thing you can feel: your feet, the seat, the air on your skin. On the third breath, notice where your attention went just now. Did it wander? Good. You noticed. That's the whole practice: the coming back.
Notice. To see what's already here, and to see where your mind just went. Third word.
Your line: where is it right now? Three times today, ask it quietly: where is my attention right now? Don't fix the answer. Just notice it, and bring it home. Day three.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY PATH ON EARTH ARRIVED AT IT ON ITS OWN.`

4.title: the rule that keeps turning up
4.hook: the rule that keeps turning up
4.tomorrow: why a sound starts and ends a sit
4.howItsDone: Most religious and ethical traditions teach some form of the golden rule; Jews often learn it through Hillel's saying, Christians through the Sermon on the Mount, and Confucians through the Analects, and many families teach it to children as their first rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: notice. Your line: where is it right now? So where was it, most of yesterday? No grade. Just the answer. Day four.

Somebody taught you this before you could read. Maybe a parent. Maybe a teacher on the playground, right after somebody grabbed something that wasn't theirs. Treat people the way you want to be treated. It's so familiar it sounds like nothing. But here's the strange part. You can find it in ancient China. In the Hebrew Bible. In the sayings of the rabbis. In the Gospels. In India's great epic, the Mahabharata. In Greek writers. It turns up on almost every path people have walked. Today's word is the golden rule.
screen: `YOU LEARNED IT BEFORE YOU COULD READ.` → `CHINA. THE BIBLE. INDIA. GREECE.` → `ALMOST EVERY PATH.`

segments.voice: Start in China, about five hundred years before the common era. A student asks Confucius if there's one word you could live by your whole life. In James Legge's translation of the Analects, Confucius answers: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Notice it's a don't. Then the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus, in among laws about harvests and fair wages, comes the line the King James renders: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Centuries later, the Talmud tells of a man who asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel says, roughly: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it. Then Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount, puts it as a do: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." India's Mahabharata has a version. So does the Greek orator Isocrates. Did every path really arrive at it on its own? Some probably did. For others, nobody can say who heard what from whom. What's clear is that it keeps turning up, and each tradition keeps it in its own place. For Confucius it's the thread of a whole life. For Hillel, a summary that sends you back to study. For Jesus, the law and the prophets in one line. The name, the golden rule, is much younger: English, from around the 1600s. One more thing. The rule starts with you. What you don't want. What you would want. It asks you to use your own heart as a map of someone else's.
screen: `CONFUCIUS: RECIPROCITY.` · `LEVITICUS: YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `HILLEL: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` · `JESUS: DO YE EVEN SO TO THEM.` · then, large: `YOUR HEART AS A MAP OF SOMEONE ELSE'S.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first breath, think of someone you'll see today. On the second, ask: if I were them, today, what would I want? Maybe to be listened to. Maybe to be left alone for a bit. Maybe just a real hello. On the third breath, let the answer settle. You don't have to do anything yet. Just know it.
The golden rule. What you'd want, given. What you'd hate, held back. Found on almost every path. Fourth word.
Your line: be good to people. Today, one person, one time: give them the thing you figured out on the second breath. Small is fine. Day four.

5.title: why a sound starts and ends a sit
5.hook: why a sound starts and ends a sit
5.tomorrow: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
5.howItsDone: Bells open and close meditation in many Buddhist communities, ring during Hindu puja, and call Christians to prayer; in Thich Nhat Hanh's communities people stop and breathe whenever any bell sounds.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the golden rule. Your line: be good to people. Who got the thing you found on the second breath? Day five.

Every session here starts with a bell and ends with one. You've heard it every day you've been here. Maybe you wondered why. It isn't decoration, and it isn't our idea. Temples in India ring bells during worship. Buddhist monasteries across Asia use bells and struck bowls to begin and end meditation. Church bells in Europe called whole villages to pray, three times a day. Some schools still run on bells. And sound reaches you in a way a picture can't. You can close your eyes. You can't close your ears. Today's word is the bell.
screen: `A BELL TO START, A BELL TO END.` → `TEMPLES, MONASTERIES, CHURCHES.` → `YOU CAN'T CLOSE YOUR EARS.`

segments.voice: Why a sound, and not a light or a word? Three reasons, from three different homes. First, a bell is a boundary. Before the bell, you were doing whatever you were doing. After it, you're here. Hindu worship, called puja, often begins with ringing a small hand bell. One traditional explanation is that the sound welcomes the divine and clears away distracting thoughts. The bell draws a line in time, and on this side of the line, something different happens. Second, a bell is shared. Before there were clocks in every pocket, one bell told a whole village at once: now. In Catholic Europe the Angelus bell rang morning, noon and evening, and people stopped to pray where they stood. There's a famous nineteenth-century painting of it by Jean-François Millet: two farm workers in a field at dusk, heads bowed. You never see the bell. You only see what it does to them. Third, a bell fades. Strike it, and the sound blooms and then slowly thins into silence, and if you follow it all the way down, you end up listening to the quiet. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught his communities to treat any bell, even a phone ringing or a clock chiming, as a call to stop, breathe, and come back to the present moment. When the bell sounded in his monasteries, people paused wherever they were, even mid-sentence, and breathed. He called it a bell of mindfulness. So a bell does three things. It marks a beginning. It gathers people. And it fades into quiet. That's why a sound starts and ends a sit here. Not to tell you what to feel. Just to say: you're here now.
screen: `A BOUNDARY IN TIME.` · `ONE SOUND, A WHOLE VILLAGE.` · `IT FADES INTO QUIET.` · `A BELL OF MINDFULNESS.` · then, large: `YOU'RE HERE NOW.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. This time, when the bell rings, don't start breathing on purpose right away. Listen to it first. Follow the sound as it thins, all the way down, until you can't tell whether you're still hearing it. Then take your three breaths into the quiet it left behind. That's arriving.
The bell. A line in time, a sound people share, a sound that fades into silence. Fifth word.
Your line: arrive. Today, pick one sound you hear often: a door, a notification, a kettle, a car starting. Every time it sounds, let it be your bell. One breath. Arrive. Day five.

screen: `DAY 5 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FEET ON THE FLOOR, HANDS ON THE KNEES.`

6.title: feet on the floor, hands on the knees
6.hook: feet on the floor, hands on the knees — you have one
6.howItsDone: Yoga, Zen and many Buddhist and Christian contemplative practices begin by settling the body: a steady, comfortable seat, feet grounded, hands at rest, with attention on how the body feels.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the bell. Your line: arrive. Which sound became your bell? Did you arrive, even once? Day six.

Quick check. Where are your feet right now? You probably had to think about it. Most of us spend the day living about a foot above our own shoulders: in a screen, in a conversation that already happened, in tomorrow's list. Meanwhile there's a whole body down here, keeping you alive, carrying you around, sending messages you mostly don't open. Feet on the floor. Hands on the knees. You have one. Almost every contemplative path, sooner or later, sends you back to it. Today's word is body.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A FOOT ABOVE YOUR SHOULDERS.` → `YOU HAVE ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with one of the oldest instructions for sitting. The Yoga Sutras, compiled in India and traditionally credited to Patanjali, say almost nothing about the poses people now call yoga. On posture they are very brief. The key line is three words in Sanskrit, and it says the seat should be steady and easy. The word is asana, and it originally meant simply a seat, the place you sit. Steady, so you're not fidgeting. Easy, so you're not straining. Early Buddhist texts put the body first too. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Satipatthana Sutta, the first thing to pay attention to is the body: breathing in, breathing out, standing, walking, sitting, lying down. Knowing, plainly, what the body is doing while it's doing it. Then, in 1890, William James made an argument that surprised his readers. Common sense says we cry because we're sad. James said it may run the other way. In his words, "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble." Psychologists have argued about how far that goes ever since, and the full story is more complicated than James thought. But one part is widely accepted: body and feeling are tangled together, and a change in one tends to show up in the other. That's part of why the body is a doorway so many paths use. You can't always choose your thoughts. You can usually choose to put your feet flat on the floor. And when you do, you're somewhere definite: here, now, on the ground. Three sources, three reasons, and none of them asks you to believe anything. They ask you to notice you're in a body.
screen: `ASANA: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.` · `MINDFULNESS STARTS WITH THE BODY.` · `AFRAID BECAUSE WE TREMBLE.` · `FEET FLAT ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `YOU'RE IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Before it rings, set your feet flat on the floor if you can, and rest your hands on your knees or in your lap. On the first breath, feel your feet. On the second, feel whatever is holding you up: the chair, the floor, the bed. On the third, feel your hands, just resting. Steady and easy. That's the whole seat.
Body. The first place so many paths ask you to notice, and the easiest one to come back to. Sixth word.
Your line: come back down. Whenever you catch yourself living up in your head today, feel your feet. One breath. Come back down. Day six.

7.title: not you
7.tomorrow: start with the person in the mirror
7.howItsDone: In many forms of meditation, people let thoughts come and go without following them, often noting them simply as "thinking" and returning to the breath; Stoic practice examines the judgments behind troubling thoughts instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: body. Your line: come back down. How many times did you catch yourself up in your head? Every catch counts. Day seven, the end of your first week.

Here's a thought for you: you left the stove on. Did you? Probably not. But for half a second, your stomach believed it. Thoughts arrive like that all day, uninvited, sounding completely sure of themselves. One large study asked people through their phones, at random moments, what they were doing and what they were thinking about. Their minds were somewhere else almost half the time. So today's hook is two words. Not you. Weather. Today's word is thoughts.
screen: `YOU LEFT THE STOVE ON.` → `ALMOST HALF THE TIME, ELSEWHERE.` → `NOT YOU. WEATHER.`

segments.voice: In 1890, William James described something everyone lives with and almost nobody had put well. He called it the stream of thought. Consciousness, he wrote, "is nothing jointed; it flows." A river, not a row of boxes. Thoughts come and go on it, and you didn't send most of them. Epictetus, the Greek teacher we met on day three, put attention to thoughts to a different use, nearly two thousand years earlier. In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." For Epictetus the trouble is less the event than the judgment we add on top of it, and that judgment, he taught, is ours to examine. Many Buddhist teachers, especially in the Tibetan tradition, use a picture you may find helpful: the mind is like the sky, and thoughts are like weather. Clouds, storms, bright spells. They move through. The sky isn't the clouds, and it isn't harmed by them. Three voices, three pictures: a stream, an opinion you can question, weather in the sky. They don't say the same thing, and they don't need to. But each one, in its own way, treats a thought as something that happens in you, not the whole of you. And look at the week you just had. Breathe. Sit. Notice. The golden rule. The bell. Body. Thoughts. Seven words, and nearly every one a way to step back an inch from the stream and see it moving. That's a real week.
screen: `IT IS NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.` · `NOT THINGS, BUT OPINIONS.` · `THE SKY AND THE WEATHER.` · `SEVEN WORDS, ONE WEEK.` · then, large: `SOMETHING THAT HAPPENS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, just breathe. On the second, wait for a thought to show up. It will. When it does, name it quietly: thinking. Don't follow it, and don't fight it. On the third breath, watch it move on, the way weather does. Then you're back here, in the body that's breathing.
Thoughts. Things that happen in you, like weather. Not the whole of you. Seventh word, and the end of week one.

Your line: let it pass. Today, when a thought shows up sounding very sure of itself, say inside: let it pass. Then feel your feet. Seven words on your strand now: breathe, sit, notice, the golden rule, the bell, body, thoughts. That's a week. Day seven.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: START WITH THE PERSON IN THE MIRROR.`
